item.title: UK tax authority plans digital ambassadors to counter AI misinformation
item.description: HMRC plans to deploy digital ambassadors on platforms such as Reddit and make official guidance easier for AI models to access, amid concerns that chatbots are spreading inaccurate tax advice ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Tom Rees The UK’s tax authorities are worried that artificial intelligence is giving people bad advice. HM Revenue & Customs is trying to stem a flood of misinformation from AI and social media, with a plan to deploy “digital ambassadors” to clearly flag correct advice in online forums such as Reddit so that browsers don’t get confused. It’s also taking steps to make official information more easily picked up by large language models. “Where sources conflict, trust falls and the risk of costly errors rises,” James Baker, head of digital communications at HMRC, told Bloomberg. “The department’s conclusion is that proactive intervention, with the right content in the right places, can shape how the wider information ecosystem responds to and corrects misinformation quickly.” AI models have been picking up erroneous information about tax, often from social media, and missing official advice from HMRC. That is then given to Britons searching for advice or amplified on sites such as TikTok.  One such example came earlier this year when search engines and AI-generated summaries were giving wrong advice about value-added tax deadlines for businesses. An investigation by HMRC traced the error to a website which had been copied to other sites, spread more widely on social media and then picked up by AI. False information such as this could have led to taxpayers missing deadlines and receiving penalties. Baker said the “episode also demonstrated how fragmented the citizen information journey has become, with people moving rapidly between search engines, AI tools, apps and social platforms.” While AI companies have warned about the risk of hallucinations or mistakes, Britons are increasingly relying on chatbots for financial advice and investments. Around three in 10 Britons have turned to such tools for financial advice, according to a survey by comparison website Finder. Social media influencers may be amplifying bad advice with videos on how viewers can cut their tax bills. Erroneous advice is a headache for UK tax authorities as they look to close the country’s £59 billion ($79 billion) tax gap — the difference between what it is owed and what it takes. Small businesses are by far the largest reason for the gap but they also may not have the expertise to spot inaccuracies in online advice.  HMRC plans to deploy officials as trusted digital ambassadors to speak to users on online forums and social media, flagging correct information. Baker said the managers will be “a proactive digital equivalent to HMRC’s broadcast spokespeople” and “help to sign post correct information and build trust.” Officials have also set up a new “HMRC Verified” strategy, an alert system aimed at countering online misinformation and guiding LLMs toward the correct advice. The large language models have responded to the changes and highlighted the correct information, according to HMRC. HMRC is also scoping out a new AI-assisted tool that could find and check claims made online against its official advice before drafting a response for a human to review and sign-off. It has issued guidance to staff to make content “LLM ready” before its launch. “Authority no longer lives on your website alone,” Baker added. “It lives in how faithfully the entire machine-readable ecosystem, from Google’s sidebar to a chatbot’s summary to a Reddit thread, repeats what you actually said.”

item.title: Meta's $25 bn penalty marks a massive win for New Mexico's attorney general
item.description: A judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in a New Mexico case stemming from a privacy scandal, an amount that dwarfs the state's projected $14.8 billion general fund revenue for fiscal 2028 ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Erik Larson, Madlin Mekelburg and Georgia Fearn With one landmark courtroom victory this week against Meta Platforms Inc., New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez is poised to bring in almost double the state’s annual revenue. A $25 billion civil penalty ordered by a judge Wednesday would be among the largest payouts in US legal history if it stands. It dwarfs the state’s $14.8 billion projected general fund revenue for fiscal year 2028. The magnitude of the windfall wasn’t lost on the Ivy League-educated official when he explained at a press conference that, by law, the money must be spent on building schools. “We may have in fact paid for the construction of schools for the next several hundred years,” Torrez said. “I don’t actually know because the amounts that we’re dealing with are so huge.” The eye-popping outcome of a case that stemmed from an almost decade-old privacy scandal is a stark example of how small-population states can have an outsized impact on Big Tech if they’re willing to risk going to trial. “When they go to trial they roll the dice,” District Judge Francis Mathew said of New Mexico at a hearing earlier this year, a nod to the risks an AG takes when dedicating massive resources to a case he could lose at trial. Torrez faced off against Meta in Santa Fe state court even after almost every other state and territory settled for far less. It’s not the first time he’s taken his chances: He won almost $1 billion from Meta earlier this year after convincing a jury that the parent of Facebook and Instagram misled youths about the dangers of predators on its social media platforms while also harming children with addictive designs. “The internet companies are bigger than most countries, in terms of their wealth,” said Eric Goldman, a law professor at Santa Clara University. “Taking that on as an individual state is a quite expensive and risky proposition.” The Democrat first elected as New Mexico’s top legal official in 2022 has taken other bold moves in court, including suing the US Justice Department in August for allegedly “stonewalling” the state’s probe into the late Jeffrey Epstein. On the same day New Mexico was awarded the equivalent of about a third of Meta’s projected fourth-quarter revenue, Torrez on Wednesday announced a new civil suit against Epstein’s former lawyer and accountant, accusing them of helping to facilitate, finance and conceal a sex trafficking operation, which allegedly included the abuse of girls and young women at the financier’s Zorro Ranch property near Santa Fe. The advisers have previously denied wrongdoing and a lawyer representing them called the suit “baseless.” In the lead-up to the $25 billion penalty, a jury determined that Meta had violated the state’s consumer protection laws over 43 million times. The September verdict was based on dozens of widely viewed statements made by the company and its top executives about how it handled hate speech and user data, including data given to Cambridge Analytica that was used to target voters for Donald Trump ahead of the 2016 election. Meta Chief Legal Officer CJ Mahoney said in a statement that “we are confident we will prevail on appeal.” “This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” Mahoney said. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online.” New Mexico went to trial alone after Meta in August agreed to pay almost half a billion dollars to other states and territories to release any future claims over Cambridge Analytica. The remaining holdouts are the District of Columbia, which has a pending suit, and Florida, which hasn’t sued. Both stand to get a boost from Torrez’s triumph. Torrez brought in outside private law firms to help with preparing and bringing the case to trial, a common tactic for small and under-resourced states. One of New Mexico’s outside trial attorneys, Corban Rhodes of the law firm DiCello Levitt, said he’s observed that the state is “not afraid to take cases to trial.”  “No matter how good a settlement is, one of the limitations is that you don’t get all the kinds of evidence out into the public record that you can with a trial,” Rhodes said. Torrez, raised in Albuquerque, earned a bachelor’s degree in government from Harvard University in 1999 and a master’s at London School of Economics before graduating from Stanford Law School in 2005. Torrez, who is married and has two children, returned to New Mexico after his education. He told Stanford Magazine in 2023 that he decided to take a job earning $37,000 a year as an assistant district attorney in New Mexico’s Valencia County, the same county where his father practiced law. Torrez went on to become a state and federal prosecutor known for handling violent crimes, firearms cases, white collar crimes, voter fraud and internet crimes against children. Former President Barack Obama appointed him as a White House fellow in 2009. His 2026 reelection campaign reflects how his profile has shifted while in office. Torrez now puts “impact litigation,” consumer protection and challenges to Big Tech at the center of his record, as national corporate cases – particularly against Meta – have become a much bigger part of his political identity. The massive Meta penalty on Wednesday is the latest result of Torrez choosing to go his own path rather than join forces with other states pursuing similar claims. In late August, Meta announced that it had struck a record-setting settlement agreement with nearly every US state for a total of $18 billion. The deal resolved an ongoing trial in Oakland, California, that pit Meta against attorneys general who alleged that the company deliberately designed Facebook and Instagram to encourage compulsive use among young users. Torrez inherited the Meta case from his predecessor, Hector Balderas, who launched the litigation over the company’s handling of personal data. Balderas said New Mexico’s willingness to pursue major companies independently rather than join national settlements dated back more than a decade, including cases against opioid manufacturers. “Our small state was not benefiting equitably in some of those national settlements,” Balderas said. He credited Torrez with continuing that approach, saying he had taken an “aggressive posture” while using litigation to push for broader changes in corporate conduct. “I am grateful to Raúl that he continued that fight.” --With assistance from Isaiah Poritz (Bloomberg Law) and Amanda Albright.

item.title: Macron takes apparent dig at Trump, Netanyahu for comments on France unrest
item.description: Speaking in Doha during a Gulf visit, the French president criticised foreign leaders for using France's recent riots for political gain, saying some were campaigning at the country's expense ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Macron takes apparent dig at Trump, Netanyahu for comments on France unrest

Macron takes apparent dig at Trump, Netanyahu for comments on France unrest Speaking in Doha during a Gulf visit, the French president criticised foreign leaders for using France's recent riots for political gain, saying some were campaigning at the country's expense

Emmanuel Macron (Photo: Reuters)

ANI Middle East 5 min read Last Updated : Oct 22 2026 | 9:05 AM IST

Listen to This Article

In an apparent swipe at US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, French President Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday strongly criticised "stupid comments" from foreign leaders for exploiting recent domestic unrest in France to further their own political campaigns. Speaking in Doha during a three-day state trip to Qatar and the broader Gulf region, aimed at securing France's energy supplies amid an ongoing national cost-of-living crisis, Macron condemned foreign figures who he said were campaigning "at France's expense" following nationwide riots over the weekend, according to Euronews. Taking aim at international counterparts without naming them directly, Macron noted that leaders on both sides of the Atlantic were in active campaign mode.

"There are people who campaign at France's expense - leaders who are in campaign mode, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic," he commented. Trump, currently campaigning ahead of the upcoming US midterm elections, has framed the French protests to highlight perceived threats surrounding immigration and Western decline. Also Read

US political campaigns tap Indian bot networks to influence voters

Ukraine would not exist without support from US, says Marco Rubio

Democrats sue Trump, US Justice Dept over effort to purge state voter rolls

Food importer sues Trump admin over 50% tariffs on Canadian goods

What are the three key issues shaping the 2026 US midterm elections?

On Monday, Trump asserted that France was "under siege, looted and set ablaze by migrants, jihadists and communists", warning American voters that similar consequences await if Democrats prevail. Rejecting claims that external interference ignited the violence, Macron called out what he termed inaccurate foreign narratives and AI-driven misinformation, according to Euronews.

"As far as I'm concerned, there is no visible foreign interference in the events that took place. There has been foreign manipulation of information in the aftermath, which led to equally unacceptable and stupid comments from many people, including foreign leaders," he said. Macron specifically denounced leaders who shared artificial intelligence-generated content depicting events that never occurred, Euronews reported. "That is to say, we've seen AI-generated images showing scenes that never actually happened in France. We have people who explained that we had been invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists", he said. When asked directly by a reporter if his remarks were directed at Donald Trump, Macron said, "Among others, yes."

Addressing reporters, the French President urged against exacerbating existing domestic tensions and defended his country's standing. "In these moments, we see who loves France and who doesn't. And the fact is, all the people who are speaking ill of our country right now are people who do not love our country. So, those people really bother me," he added. While mass demonstrations organised by trade unions, the Yellow Vest movement, and student groups saw mostly peaceful marches over the weekend, widespread looting and clashes with law enforcement on Saturday overshadowed the protests. According to Euronews, President Macron confirmed he will convene an emergency meeting with cabinet ministers and intelligence officials on Thursday to receive a "detailed account" of the October 17 events upon returning to Paris.

His remarks come after US President Donald Trump on Monday (local time) claimed that Paris would soon become a "Muslim city", criticising Macron for not closing the country's borders, blaming immigration for the ongoing widespread protests in Paris. Speaking to reporters outside the White House, Trump said the protests and violence in France were linked to immigration rather than education or domestic policy issues, warning that European countries faced serious consequences if they failed to tighten border controls and deport people he described as criminals. "Well, France, it is a very sad situation what's happening in France, because what's happening in France has to do with immigration, not schools, not anything. It's immigration," Trump said.

Referring to his relationship with Macron, Trump said the French President was a friend but had made a mistake by allowing people from across the world to enter France. "And, as you know, Paris is going to be a Muslim city very soon. And that wasn't the deal. That wasn't the deal. I told Emmanuel, you should close up your borders," Trump added. On the other hand, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu asserted on Tuesday that France is confronting an "invasion of extremist Islam". As reported by Times of Israel, during an interview with French-language network i24News, the Israeli Prime Minister criticised French authorities for failing to adequately anticipate the disorder and alleged that radical Muslim groups drove the turmoil, notwithstanding the broad and diverse cross-section of French citizens participating in the demonstrations.

Directly targeting the French government's response to the situation, Netanyahu stated. "They did not prepare in time; they simply gave up. They succumbed to the invasion of extremist Islam." Asked what advice he would give to France, Netanyahu said: "Fight back, do not pursue a policy of appeasement - fight against the extremists." This comes amid continued unrest in France, where authorities have introduced curfews and stepped up security measures following violent disturbances and looting. In Bordeaux, local authorities announced a week-long night curfew for unaccompanied minors following widespread looting and violence in the city centre over the weekend. The order, announced on Monday by Sophie Brocas, Prefect of Gironde and Nouvelle-Aquitaine, will remain in effect from Tuesday until the morning of October 26. It restricts minors under the age of 18 from being in public spaces between 10 pm and 7 am unless accompanied by a parent or legal guardian.

The measure follows riots on October 17, which officials described as involving an "unprecedented level of violence". Several thousand rioters targeted commercial areas in central Bordeaux, smashing storefronts and ransacking shops. Authorities deployed 400 police officers and gendarmes, supported by two water cannons and two armoured vehicles, to contain the violence. Nearly 120 people were arrested over Saturday and Sunday and face prosecution. At least 2,400 people were arrested following the unrest, which saw town halls set on fire and hundreds of businesses looted or damaged, according to the report.

item.title: Asian markets slip, led by South Korea, despite upbeat US tech earnings
item.description: MSCI's Asia-Pacific index outside Japan fell 0.2%, while South Korean shares dropped over 1%. Concerns over AI spending and Gulf tensions offset stronger-than-expected US technology earnings ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / Markets / Commodities / Asian markets slip, led by South Korea, despite upbeat US tech earnings

Asian markets slip, led by South Korea, despite upbeat US tech earnings MSCI's Asia-Pacific index outside Japan fell 0.2%, while South Korean shares dropped over 1%. Concerns over AI spending and Gulf tensions offset stronger-than-expected US technology earnings

Image: Bloomberg

Reuters HONG KONG 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 22 2026 | 8:13 AM IST

Listen to This Article

Asian stocks struggled to stay above water in early trade on Thursday, as tech earnings optimism provided only fleeting support amid lingering concerns over AI and uncertainty in the Gulf. MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan was down 0.2 per cent, on track for a fourth straight week of decline. Japan's Nikkei stock index gave up earlier gains to trade 0.4 per cent lower, while Korean shares were down more than 1 per cent. US stock futures, the S&P 500 e-minis, were down 0.4 per cent at 7,765.8. Overnight, the tech-heavy Nasdaq led Wall Street to a higher close as better-than-expected earnings reports from market heavyweights helped ease some concerns over the sustainability and profitability of massive AI build-outs.

Space X posted its first profit as a public company, Meta reported third-quarter revenue that beat expectations, while AI server maker Super Micro forecast quarterly revenue and profit margin that both topped estimates. However, Meta's plan to issue non-voting Class C common stock drew renewed scrutiny on AI spending. Also Read

Stocks to watch: BEL, Swiggy, Eternal, IHCL, PC Jeweller, RBL Bank, SRF

Stock Market Close: Sensex falls for 2nd day, ends 143 pts down, Nifty at 22,811; VIX surges 6%

Asian shares climb, bonds stabilise as strong earnings buoy Wall Street

Asian stocks skid on AI worries, Wall Street and bonds aided by oil slip

Earnings, crude oil, Jio IPO key monitorables for investors next week

"There's a lot of noise out there at the moment and investors are still digesting this morning's results," said Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com. "Also, we're really only at the start of the meaty part of earnings season, which is coming at the same time that investors are tackling the uncertainty from an upcoming Fed decision, geopolitical risks, and US mid-terms."

In a sign of subdued risk sentiment, the yield on benchmark 10-year Treasury notes was down 4.2 basis points at 5.1065 per cent, while the yield on 30-year notes was at a one-week low of 5.3968 per cent. Meanwhile, Brent crude rose 1.1 per cent to $110.03 a barrel, near a five-month high. The US ordered diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia amid Houthi strikes, while the New York Times reported the US and Israeli militaries had developed specific plans for renewed attacks on Iran after the US midterm elections, which take place on November 3. In currencies, the dollar index, which tracks the greenback against a basket of currencies of other major trading partners, dipped to 102.2. The euro was little changed at $1.1231.

The yen was also flat at 158.125, after Deputy Bank of Japan Governor Ryozo Himino signalled his readiness to raise borrowing costs. The Korean won was muted at 1325.9, after the Bank of Korea left its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 3.00 per cent on Thursday. Gold was slightly lower at $4115.5 per ounce. [GOL/] Bitcoin was down 0.4 per cent at $84,284.05, while ether was 0.6 per cent lower at $2,476.34.
